  "summary": "S1 — Fact: deliver a small browser-playable Battleship game for one person against the computer; the browser and the Node.js-served game are the intended entry points. Recorded defaults: use conventional Battleship rules, an anonymous session to identify the player, and temporary game state for one browser session; restarting or ending the game clears that state, and state is not shared across people, devices, or sessions. Keep the computer's unhit ship locations hidden from the player during play. These defaults rule out accounts, shared or persistent games, and rule variants unless later evidence establishes they are needed. Open runtime question: discovery must first establish what the browser and server environment already provide, which blocks the choice of session and state implementation; no runtime capabilities are verified by the request. Fact: the repository is empty; no team, workspace, channel, internal site, document, private repository, owner, or ambiguous-term source hint was supplied. Any sensitive locator discovered later belongs only in an authorized private store, not committed KNOWLEDGE/. The isolated source checkout remains at its snapshot until final return, when the result becomes visible there; a deployed outcome would be visible only after release, and no deployment target is named. S2 — Fact: use Node.js for the server and include tests. Open tooling question: discovery must first establish the available Node.js version and test facilities, which blocks selection of compatible commands and APIs; recorded default: use Node.js's built-in test facilities when supported. Fact: this stage is intake only, implementation is outside its scope, and no person is available to answer questions during the run."
